clue.text: Cheap fare provider carrying airline's frequent fliers in prime locations

indicators.note: prime locations are the leading positions, so each word contributes its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter of carrying
first letter of airline's
first letter of frequent
first letter of fliers

explanation.surface: A budget airline whose regular passengers get the best seats.
explanation.walkthrough: A CAFF is British slang for a cheap, basic café, such as a roadside transport café. The surface makes 'fare' sound like a ticket price.
explanation.definitionFit: A caff is an inexpensive eatery, so it supplies cheap food, punning on fare as both meals and ticket price.

clue.text: Roman conspirator screening a mostly banal film

indicators.note: screening means hiding behind or around, so the conspirator encloses the rest
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: Casca was one of Julius Caesar's assassins
taken as written
banal and bland both mean dull

explanation.surface: A Roman plotter sits through a fairly dull movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screening' sounds like showing a film, which suits the surface; it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Casablanca is the 1942 Bogart and Bergman classic, an example of a film.

clue.text: Member is fine, if not lamenting work endlessly

indicators.note: without its end, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
or, meaning otherwise
an elegy is a poem of lament

explanation.surface: A club member is doing fine, as long as they are not grieving over endless work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a person in a club; here it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A member is a limb of the body, and a foreleg is a front limb of an animal.

clue.text: Badgers and monkeys crossing one rut shakily

indicators.note: to cross something here is to straddle it, so the monkeys sit either side of the other letters
something done shakily is unsteady and disordered, so the preceding letters are jumbled

blocks.note: monkeys as in mischievous children, imps
the letters of one and rut rearranged

explanation.surface: Animals in the wild: badgers and monkeys stumbling across a rutted track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badgers' looks like a noun in a list of animals with monkeys; it is the verb, and monkeys is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger someone is to pester them persistently, which is exactly what importuning means.

clue.text: I see teacher returning greeting by male teacher of distinction

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so that word is read backwards
by means next to, so the abbreviation is placed alongside the rest

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
aha is an exclamation of understanding
schoolchildren address a male teacher as sir
hi is an informal greeting

explanation.surface: A pupil acknowledges a male teacher passing by with a hello.
explanation.walkthrough: The male piece goes first in the answer although it comes last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharishi is a Hindu sage or great spiritual guide, literally a great seer.

clue.text: Group books houses and suchlike to the north

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it inside, so the books surround the next piece
in a down clue, heading north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: OT, the Old Testament, is a collection of books
etc, et cetera, means and suchlike

explanation.surface: A group books accommodation, houses and so forth, somewhere up north.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a set of eight, a musical or other group.

clue.text: Agitators in time meeting Moscow Mint employees?

indicators.note: meeting means coming up against, so the two pieces are joined end to end

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the Russian mint's workers make roubles, Russia's currency

explanation.surface: Political agitators turn up to meet the staff at the Russian mint.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented phrase: mint workers make money, and in Moscow that money is roubles.
explanation.definitionFit: Troublemakers stir up unrest, which is what agitators do.

clue.text: What suggests Mother Superior's part of London

blocks.note: a Mother is a nun in charge of a convent
a superior is a head or chief

explanation.surface: A riddle: which London district does a convent's Mother Superior call to mind?
explanation.walkthrough: A Mother Superior is the head nun of a convent, so the name splits into those two words. Nunhead is a district of south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Nunhead is a district in the London Borough of Southwark, so it is literally a part of the capital.

clue.text: Following revolution, party moderates feel agitation

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: wets are moderate members of the British Conservative party, a label from the Thatcher era

explanation.surface: After an uprising, the party's moderates are nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: To stew is to fret or worry anxiously, a state of agitation.

clue.text: Beside edges of tablecloth spread crumbs

indicators.note: beside places one piece alongside the next, joining them in sequence
the edges of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

blocks.note: to strew is to scatter or spread
first and last letters of tablecloth

explanation.surface: Clearing up after a meal: crumbs scattered next to the tablecloth's edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbs' reads as bits of bread, but it is the mild exclamation of surprise, like STREWTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British exclamations of surprise or dismay, so one interjection substitutes for the other.

clue.text: After game, large English fan, say, is a critic of foul play

indicators.note: after places the following pieces behind the first one in sequence

blocks.note: whist is a card game
L is the abbreviation for large
E is the abbreviation for English
a fan is an example of a blower, a device that pushes air

explanation.surface: After the match a big English supporter complains about foul play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan' reads as a supporter of the game; it is an air-blowing device.
explanation.definitionFit: A whistleblower exposes wrongdoing inside an organisation, publicly condemning foul play.

clue.text: Turning right, cat getting cream

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the abbreviation is read backwards

blocks.note: RT is a standard abbreviation for right
the ounce is another name for the snow leopard

explanation.surface: A cat swerves to the right on its way to the cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' suggests a saucer for the cat, but here it is the slang verb meaning to beat heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To cream an opponent is informal for defeating them overwhelmingly, the same sense as trounce.

clue.text: Will criminal triad with brains potter around this?

indicators.note: criminal suggests the following word is crooked, bent out of its proper order

blocks.note: Will and Bill are both short forms of William
the letters of triad rearranged
someone with brains is able, clever

explanation.surface: Will a gangster with brains loiter around here? A question about a seedy hangout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' looks like the verb to dawdle; it is a player who pots balls, and the table is what they move around.
explanation.definitionFit: A snooker or billiards player who pots balls walks around the table, so the table is where a potter circles.

clue.text: Probably dressing like head of Armani in extravagant fashion

indicators.note: dressing something means wrapping clothes around it, so the outer word encloses the others
'head of' keeps only the first letter of 'Armani'

blocks.note: prolly is a slangy contraction of probably
to dig something is slang for liking it
first letter of Armani

explanation.surface: Wearing something Armani-ish is likely an extravagant way to dress.
explanation.walkthrough: PROLLY is very informal internet slang for probably, surprising in The Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigally means wastefully lavish, spending without restraint, which is acting in an extravagant manner.

clue.text: Are contracts obtained giving special terms?

indicators.note: a word that contracts gets shorter, so it loses its final letter

blocks.note: are with its last letter dropped
got is the past tense of get, to obtain

explanation.surface: A question about whether signed contracts include special conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracts' looks like a noun for agreements, which suits 'special terms'; it is a verb telling you to shorten the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the jargon or slang of a particular group, the special vocabulary its members use.

clue.text: Bit of elastic in hem for undies consumer grabs

indicators.note: a hem is the border of a garment, so only the edge letters of the next word are kept
to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece closes around the other

blocks.note: a consumer is someone who spends
first and last letters of undies

explanation.surface: A shopper snatching underwear that has elastic in its hem.
explanation.walkthrough: The undies are inserted after the first letter of the consumer.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspender is an elastic strap that holds up a stocking or sock, so it is a piece of elastic.

clue.text: Influential banks providing a bit of competition

indicators.note: banks are the sides of a river, so the outer word lines both sides of the inserted pair

blocks.note: seminal means highly influential
providing means on condition that, if

explanation.surface: Powerful banks supply a little rivalry in the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' reads as financial institutions; it is a verb meaning to flank.
explanation.definitionFit: A semifinal is one round of a knockout tournament, so it is one part of a competition.

clue.text: Moaned this person twice knocked back life advice

indicators.note: something knocked back is pushed backwards, so those letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: to carp is to complain or moan
the setter refers to himself two ways, as me and as I

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about being rebuffed twice when offering advice on how to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This person' is the setter, who can be ME or I; both are needed here, then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpe diem, Latin for seize the day, is a motto urging people to make the most of life now.

clue.text: Group serving meat cut for British colonialist

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the final letter is trimmed off

blocks.note: the RAF is the Royal Air Force, an armed service
flesh is meat

explanation.surface: A catering team serving sliced meat to a British empire builder.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Stamford Raffles founded modern Singapore in 1819.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffles was an administrator of the British Empire in Southeast Asia, a famous colonial figure.

clue.text: Was a ham scoffed by daughter around 4th of March?

indicators.note: by places one item next to another, so the abbreviation follows directly
around means surrounding, so the earlier letters wrap the selected one
the ordinal tells you which single letter of the month's name to take

blocks.note: to scoff food is to eat it greedily
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
the fourth letter of March

explanation.surface: Did the daughter eat the ham around early March?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like meat that was scoffed; it is an over-the-top performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham is a showy, overacting performer, so being a ham means having acted, theatrically and badly.

clue.text: Fantastic plant's amazing, finally five times bigger

indicators.note: the last letter, read as a Roman numeral, is swapped for the numeral worth five times as much

blocks.note: a slangy spelling of terrific, how the word is often said

explanation.surface: An enthusiast praises a wonder plant that grows to five times its size.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter C is Roman 100; five times that is 500, written D.
explanation.definitionFit: Triffids are the walking, man-eating plants of John Wyndham's novel, so a fictional, fantastical plant.

clue.text: Base rate cuts bringing down a valued bond

indicators.note: something that cuts into another thing pushes inside it, so these letters go into the middle

blocks.note: felling is cutting down or bringing down, as with trees
base means low
a rate or charge is a fee

explanation.surface: Central bank interest rate cuts depress the value of a bond.
explanation.walkthrough: The financial vocabulary is all false: base rate and bond suggest the Bank of England, but the bond here is sympathy between people.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow feeling is sympathy arising from shared experience, a cherished connection between people.

clue.text: Dealing with wrapping paper close to Yule in many cases

indicators.note: wrapping means enclosing, so the first word goes round the others
the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is used

blocks.note: on means about or concerning
the FT is the Financial Times newspaper
last letter of Yule

explanation.surface: Wrapping Christmas presents, frequently near Yuletide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrapping paper' looks like gift wrap; wrapping is the container signal and paper the newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means frequently, happening on many occasions.

clue.text: Dull sound of one day following another

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first piece is placed after the second

blocks.note: Thu is the abbreviation for Thursday, another day
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: Monotony of one day after another making a dull noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are days: D as the abbreviation for day, THU for Thursday.
explanation.definitionFit: A thud is a heavy, muffled noise, a low dull sound.

clue.text: Prince with attractive clothes, a simple fellow

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here: to clothe something is to wrap it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare
fit is British slang for good-looking
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' reads as a plural noun; it is the verb, with attractive wrapped around with.
explanation.definitionFit: A halfwit is a foolish or dim person, which is what a simple fellow means.

clue.text: Amount of fish bearing small amount of eggs

indicators.note: bearing means carrying, so the first piece holds the abbreviation inside it

blocks.note: a netful is as many fish as a net holds
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A quantity of fish carrying a few eggs, as with roe.
explanation.definitionFit: A nestful is as many as a nest holds, a natural measure for a clutch of eggs.

clue.text: Hack off nose of Stilton with swinish remark in fancy deli

indicators.note: the nose is the front, so only the opening letter of the cheese is used
with joins two pieces together side by side
in places those letters inside the rearranged shop word
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the following word is rearranged

blocks.note: deli with its letters rearranged
first letter of Stilton
a grunt is the noise a pig makes

explanation.surface: A customer cuts off the end of a Stilton with a rude snort in a posh delicatessen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack off' reads like slicing cheese; it is British slang for annoy. Stilton is an English blue cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: To be hacked off is to be fed up, so to hack someone off is to annoy or disgruntle them.

clue.text: Bear losing face in current disruption

indicators.note: losing its face means losing its front, so the opening letter goes
